questions.q: What does read_and_clean() do before any data is sent to Snowflake?
options: It uploads the raw CSV directly without modification
It reads the CSV with pandas, drops rows missing required columns, and fixes types like converting sent_at to a real datetime
It connects to Snowflake and creates the target table
It deletes the CSV file from disk
questions.explain: pd.read_csv, dropna, and type fixes (pd.to_datetime, astype(bool)) all happen before the script ever touches Snowflake.

questions.q: What does cur.executemany(...) do in load_to_snowflake()?
options: It runs a single SELECT to preview the data
It runs the same parameterized INSERT statement once per row, loading every cleaned row in one batch call
It creates multiple Snowflake warehouses
It executes the script multiple times in parallel
questions.explain: executemany runs the parameterized INSERT across every row in the cleaned dataframe in a single batch operation.

questions.q: Why does this script connect using role="transformer" instead of creating a dedicated new ingestion role?
options: Snowflake does not allow Python scripts to specify a role
Reusing the existing transformer role keeps the RBAC story from Chapter 2 simple, instead of creating a sprawl of narrowly-scoped roles nobody tracks
transformer is the only role capable of running Python code
A new role would have required rebuilding the entire warehouse
questions.explain: This script writes into the same RAW schema dbt itself reads from, under the same role Chapter 2 already set up — no new access model needed.

questions.q: How should a developer confirm this script's load actually worked?
options: Trust the script's own print statement with no further check
Run a real SELECT COUNT(*) and a sample SELECT against raw_campaign_sends in Snowflake directly
Assume success if the script exits without an error dialog
Check only that the CSV file still exists on disk
questions.explain: The same verification habit from Lesson 4's COPY INTO loads applies — check real rows in Snowflake, not just the script's own reported output.

questions.q: Why does load_to_snowflake() read Snowflake credentials from os.environ rather than hardcoding them in the script?
options: Python cannot store string literals longer than 20 characters
Hardcoding credentials directly in a committed script file would expose real secrets — the same env_var-style pattern used elsewhere in this platform's profiles.yml
os.environ runs faster than a literal string
It has no real benefit; it's purely a style preference
questions.explain: Reading credentials from environment variables keeps secrets out of the script file, consistent with how profiles.yml avoids hardcoding them too.
